# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review: Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week (Varden County)

This is a much stronger study than the pilot in the previous working paper. It fixes most of the problems I raised there:
- It has a randomised control group.
- Output comes from administrative records, not manager ratings.
- Hours come from timesheets.
- The analysis plan was registered.
- Coverage-bound work is analysed separately.
- The exploratory analysis is clearly labelled as exploratory.

Its own finding that scheduled-hours accounting turns +12.5% into +22% puts a number on the bias that made the pilot's +23.4% unreliable.

The arithmetic checks out. Hours fell 12.9% and 17.0%. Output per hour is 0.979/0.871 ≈ +12.4% and 0.886/0.830 ≈ +6.7%. The scheduled-hours version is 0.979/0.8 ≈ +22%. The output-per-FTE confidence intervals are symmetric as expected.

The remaining issues are mostly about inference with so few clusters, outcomes that are reported less rigorously than the primary one, and how the per-hour figures should be interpreted.

## 1. Inference with 14 and 10 clusters

Cluster-robust standard errors with 10 clusters (5 v 5) are known to be anti-conservative. The paper doesn't say whether a small-sample correction was used. Options include CR2 with *t*(G−1) critical values, the wild cluster bootstrap, or randomisation inference, which this design supports naturally.

This matters most for the counter stratum's output per hour, +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3). The lower bound is barely above zero, and a proper few-cluster correction would likely push it below zero. The Discussion's statement that "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" rests on that interval.

A smaller oddity: if hours were fixed at −17%, the output-per-FTE interval implies a per-hour interval of about +0.1% to +13.4%. Because hours are also estimated, the reported interval should be at least that wide, not narrower. That is possible only if hours and output covary across offices. It's worth explaining how the per-hour intervals were computed.

## 2. The per-hour gain in counter offices is largely queueing arithmetic

In coverage-bound work, output depends on demand. When fewer staff cover the same opening hours, queues lengthen: waits rose 64% and abandoned calls went from 6% to 10%. Each remaining staff member therefore spends less time idle between contacts. Contacts handled per hour worked rise mechanically through higher utilisation, even if nobody works faster or better.

So the +6.7% should not be described as workers being "more productive." It is at least partly a measure of slack being absorbed by the public's waiting time. The paper's broader point, that productivity per hour and per employee come apart, is correct. This mechanism actually strengthens it, but the paper should name the mechanism rather than credit it to the workers.

## 3. Secondary outcomes don't get the primary outcome's rigour

Table 1 is titled "difference-in-differences estimates," but several rows are not DiD estimates:

| Outcome | What is actually reported |
|---|---|
| Overturn rate / repeat contacts | Treated v control levels; no pre-period, no CI |
| Average wait | Treated offices only, pre → month 9; no control comparison |
| Abandoned calls (text only) | Treated only; not in the registered outcome list; not flagged as unregistered |
| Sick days | Pooled across strata; no CI |
| Resignations | Not registered; no pre-period; no CI (imprecision is acknowledged) |

Two consequences follow:
- The conclusion that case-processing quality was "unchanged" rests on 3.1% v 3.0% with no interval.
- The conclusion that counter service was worse rests on figures from treated offices only.

Both conclusions are plausible, but they should be estimated the same way as the primary outcome. The authors flag the unregistered meetings analysis carefully. The same flag should go on abandoned calls and resignations.

## 4. Case-processing output may hide backlog and case mix

"Cases closed" with a −2.1% point estimate is consistent with other changes the paper doesn't measure:
- **Backlog growth.** If inflow was unchanged, a shortfall in closures accumulates. The paper should report queue size, case age, and the rate of statutory-deadline breaches. The Limitations section raises backlog risk, but the data to check it should already exist in the case-management system.
- **Cherry-picking.** Under time pressure, staff can close simple cases first. Weighting output by case complexity, or reporting the case-type mix, would rule this out.
- **Appeal lag.** Decisions made late in the nine months may not have been appealed yet, so the overturn rate could understate any quality effect.

## 5. Spillovers between arms

Randomising by office prevents contamination between colleagues, but not between workloads:
- **Call routing.** Contact-centre telephone lines are often routed across sites. If calls overflowed from short-staffed treated centres to control centres, control workload rose and the estimated difference is distorted.
- **Shared queues.** If benefits or permit cases sit in county-wide queues, cases could be reallocated between offices.

The paper should state whether queues and phone lines are office-specific.

## 6. Hours and cost

- **Unrecorded hours.** Timesheets capture *claimed* overtime. Unclaimed work, such as finishing cases from home, would make the per-hour gain an overstatement again, by the same logic the paper applies to scheduled hours.
- **Cost.** Treated case-processing staff averaged about 3 hours a week of claimed overtime on top of full pay for 30 hours. If that overtime is paid at a premium, cost per case closed probably *rose*, even though output per employee barely moved. The county's stated question was whether the change could be made "without loss of service." Cost per unit of output belongs alongside the productivity measures.

## 7. Exploratory meetings analysis

The analysis is well caveated, but it has a problem the caveats don't cover. Calendar data were collected only in month six. The paper can therefore compare meeting *levels* between arms, but it cannot measure how much each office *cut* its meetings. The claim that "offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains" needs pre-period calendar data, and the paper doesn't say it has any.

Also, with *n* = 7, a correlation of r = 0.71 has a 95% interval of roughly −0.03 to 0.95 (p ≈ 0.07). It's good that a confirmatory test has been registered for 24 months. That test should measure meeting time before and after the change, in both arms.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Heterogeneity test.** The stratum split was pre-specified, which is good. But the difference between −2.1% and −11.4% should be tested formally with an interaction term, not just shown by non-overlapping intervals.
- **Pooled estimate.** If the registered primary analysis was pooled, report the pooled estimate.
- **Why the strata differ.** The two strata differ in more than presence-dependence: public contact, staff composition, and management. "What matters is whether output depends on presence" is the most plausible explanation, but this design cannot isolate it.
- **The counter result reflects one implementation.** It describes cutting hours with no extra staff and opening hours unchanged. Hiring to restore cover, or changing opening hours, would produce different results. A sentence saying so would stop readers over-generalising in the opposite direction.
- **Wellbeing trajectory.** Novelty is mentioned. Reporting sick days and any survey measures at months 3, 6 and 9 would show whether there was a decay like the one in the pilot.

## Summary

The design is sound and the Discussion's main conclusions are largely supported:
- Output per employee was maintained in backlog-type work.
- Output per employee fell, and service got worse, in coverage-bound work.
- Per-hour figures based on scheduled hours are inflated.

To make the paper fully defensible:
1. Use few-cluster inference throughout.
2. Bring the secondary outcomes up to the same DiD-with-intervals standard and flag the unregistered ones.
3. Reinterpret the counter per-hour gain as a utilisation effect.
4. Add backlog, case-mix and cost measures.
5. Address possible spillovers between arms.
6. Fix the "cut most" claim in the meetings analysis.

I can draft revised wording for the Discussion or Table 1, or a short comparison of the two papers, if useful.
